title: Phishing Fundamentals and the Credential-Harvesting Lifecycle
text:
Phishing is a social-engineering attack in which an adversary impersonates a trusted person, brand, or service to trick a victim into revealing sensitive information or taking a harmful action. It is catalogued in the MITRE ATT&CK framework as technique T1566. The goal is most often credential theft, but phishing is also used to deliver malware, authorize fraudulent payments, or harvest one-time passcodes in real time.

A typical credential-harvesting campaign follows a predictable lifecycle. First, the attacker registers or compromises a domain and stands up a fake login page that mimics a legitimate brand. Second, they craft a lure - an email, text message, or chat - that creates a plausible pretext and a sense of urgency. Third, they distribute the lure at scale or to selected targets. Fourth, when a victim clicks through and enters their credentials, those values are captured and either used immediately or sold.

Modern phishing increasingly defeats basic multi-factor authentication using reverse-proxy toolkits that sit between the victim and the real site, relaying the login in real time and stealing the resulting session cookie. This is why phishing-resistant authentication and user vigilance both remain important even when MFA is enabled.

The defining characteristic of phishing is deception about identity or intent. Every detection signal - suspicious sender, lookalike domain, urgency language, mismatched links - is ultimately evidence that the message is not what it claims to be.

title: Email Phishing: Common Indicators in Message Content
text:
Phishing emails share recurring content patterns that distinguish them from legitimate correspondence. The most reliable is manufactured urgency: warnings that an account will be suspended, a payment has failed, or a package cannot be delivered unless the recipient acts immediately. Urgency is designed to short-circuit careful judgment.

Generic or impersonal greetings such as 'Dear Customer' or 'Dear User' are common because attackers send the same template to many recipients and rarely know individual names. Legitimate services that hold an account relationship usually address the customer by name.

Requests to verify, confirm, or re-enter credentials, payment details, or personal data are a strong signal. Reputable organizations do not ask users to confirm passwords by email. Threats of negative consequences, offers that seem too good to be true, and unexpected attachments or links round out the pattern.

Language and formatting anomalies - awkward grammar, inconsistent branding, low-resolution logos, or mismatched fonts - can indicate a hastily assembled template, though well-funded campaigns now produce polished messages, so their absence does not prove legitimacy. The safest posture is to treat any unsolicited message that pressures you to click a link or disclose information as suspect until verified through an independent channel.

title: Sender Spoofing, Display-Name Deception, and Reply-To Mismatch
text:
Email is trivially forgeable at the surface level because the visible 'From' name and the underlying sending address are separate fields. Display-name deception sets the friendly name to a trusted brand or executive while the actual address belongs to an unrelated or throwaway domain. On mobile clients that hide the full address, this is highly effective.

A related trick is the reply-to mismatch: the message appears to come from a legitimate address, but the Reply-To header points elsewhere, so any response goes to the attacker. Cousin or lookalike sending domains - a legitimate-looking variant such as a hyphenated or misspelled version of a real domain - are also widely used.

Header analysis exposes much of this. The Received chain reveals the true origin servers, and authentication results (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) indicate whether the sending domain authorized the message. A failed or absent DMARC alignment on a message claiming to be from a major brand is a strong fraud signal.

Because the human-visible cues can be faked, defenders rely on a combination of header authentication and content analysis rather than trusting the displayed sender alone.

title: Spear Phishing and Business Email Compromise (BEC)
text:
Spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalized lures built from reconnaissance - job title, projects, colleagues, vendors, or social-media activity. Because the message references real context, it is far more convincing than bulk phishing and far harder to detect with generic filters.

Business Email Compromise is a high-value subclass in which the attacker impersonates an executive, supplier, or trusted partner to authorize a fraudulent action, most commonly a wire transfer or a change of banking details. BEC frequently uses no malicious link or attachment at all, relying purely on authority, urgency, and plausible pretext, which is why URL- and attachment-based detection misses it.

Common BEC scenarios include the urgent CEO request for a confidential payment, the vendor invoice with newly 'updated' bank details, and the payroll-diversion request to redirect an employee's direct deposit. Thread hijacking - replying within a genuine, previously compromised email thread - makes these especially credible.

The primary defenses are procedural: out-of-band verification of payment and banking changes, dual authorization for transfers, and treating any unexpected change of financial instructions as suspect regardless of who appears to have sent it.

title: Malicious URLs: Typosquatting and Lookalike Domains
text:
Attackers register domains that closely resemble a legitimate brand so that a hurried reader accepts them as genuine. Typosquatting exploits common keyboard errors - a transposed, doubled, or omitted character, such as a brand name missing one letter. Combosquatting appends plausible words to a real brand, producing domains like brand-security or brand-login that contain the genuine name but are not owned by it.

Other variants include alternate top-level domains (a real brand name under an unexpected or cheap TLD), subdomain abuse where the trusted brand name is placed in a subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain, and bit-squatting that relies on rare memory errors. The unifying tactic is to borrow visual or textual trust from a known name.

A crucial reading skill is identifying the registrable domain - the portion immediately to the left of the public suffix. Everything before it, including reassuring words and additional subdomains, is attacker-controlled and carries no guarantee of identity. A link reading login.bank.example-secure.com belongs to example-secure.com, not to the bank.

Detection combines lexical features of the hostname with reputation and similarity scoring against known brands, since no single character pattern is conclusive on its own.

title: Homograph and Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) Attacks
text:
Internationalized Domain Names allow non-ASCII characters in hostnames, which legitimately supports the world's writing systems but also enables homograph attacks. Many characters in scripts such as Cyrillic or Greek are visually identical or near-identical to Latin letters; a Cyrillic 'a' renders the same as a Latin 'a' to the human eye but is a different code point, so the domain resolves somewhere entirely different.

IDNs are encoded for DNS using Punycode, producing an ASCII representation prefixed with xn--. A domain that looks like a familiar brand but whose Punycode form reveals mixed or unexpected scripts is a strong indicator of a homograph attack. Mixed-script labels - combining characters from more than one alphabet within a single label - are especially suspicious.

Browsers mitigate this by displaying the Punycode form when a label mixes scripts or matches risky patterns, but display behavior is inconsistent across clients, so users cannot rely on it alone.

Automated defenses decode the hostname, check whether it is an IDN, detect script mixing, and compare the rendered form against known brand names. Flagging a domain as an internationalized or homograph lookalike is informational context that strengthens an overall verdict rather than a standalone proof of malice, since legitimate internationalized domains also exist.

title: URL Shorteners, Redirect Chains, and Link Obfuscation
text:
Link shorteners and redirect chains hide a URL's true destination behind an opaque or trusted-looking intermediary. A shortened link gives the reader no information about where it leads, and attackers exploit this to mask credential-harvesting pages. Open redirects on legitimate domains are abused similarly: a trusted domain is used as the visible host, but a redirect parameter forwards the victim to a malicious site, lending the link borrowed credibility.

Multi-hop redirect chains chain several of these together, sometimes inserting conditional logic that shows benign content to security scanners and malicious content to real users. The final landing page is what matters for a verdict, so resolving the chain to its endpoint is essential.

Safe resolution follows redirects server-side, with strict limits on the number of hops and timeouts, while guarding against server-side request forgery by refusing to fetch internal or private network addresses. The resolved final URL, the full redirect chain, and whether a known shortener was involved are all useful features.

Note that browsers often follow protocol upgrades and short redirects before a client-side tool observes the final tab, so redirect detection is most reliable as a server-side capability operating on the originally submitted link rather than on the address a browser has already settled on.

title: Newly Registered and Short-Lived Domains as Risk Signals
text:
Domain age is a meaningful risk signal because a large share of phishing infrastructure is disposable. Attackers register domains in bulk, use them for a short campaign, and abandon them before reputation systems catch up. A domain registered only days ago that is already hosting a login form for an established brand is inherently suspicious, since real brands operate long-lived, well-known domains.

The activation or registration date can be estimated from WHOIS or RDAP records, or from passive DNS observations of when a name first became active. A common practical threshold treats domains younger than roughly thirty days as elevated risk, though the exact cutoff is a tuning decision.

Freshness is a probabilistic indicator, not a verdict. Legitimate new businesses register new domains every day, and some malicious sites operate on long-aged but compromised domains. For that reason, domain age is best used as an overlay that raises or lowers confidence in combination with other signals, rather than as a sole basis for blocking.

When presented to a user, a recently-registered notice explains part of the reasoning behind a cautious verdict and helps them understand why an otherwise ordinary-looking link warrants extra care.

title: Credential-Harvesting Pages and Brand Impersonation
text:
The destination of most phishing links is a credential-harvesting page: a counterfeit login screen that imitates a trusted brand to capture usernames, passwords, and second factors. Frequently impersonated brands include major email and cloud providers, banks, payment services, shipping companies, and tax authorities, because these accounts are valuable and widely held.

These pages often clone the visual design of the real site pixel-for-pixel, sometimes by directly copying the target's HTML and assets. Telltale signals include a hostname unrelated to the brand, a form that submits to a different domain than the one displayed, missing or invalid HTTPS, and prompts for information a legitimate login would never request up front, such as full card numbers or recovery codes.

Advanced kits proxy the real login in real time to defeat MFA, capturing the live session token after the victim completes authentication. Others present a fake MFA prompt to harvest one-time codes directly.

The strongest user defense is to never enter credentials on a page reached by clicking an emailed or messaged link. Navigating to the service independently - via a bookmark or by typing the known address - removes the attacker's controlled entry point entirely.

title: Attachment-Based Phishing and HTML Smuggling
text:
Some phishing campaigns deliver their payload as an attachment rather than a link. Malicious documents may carry macros, embedded scripts, or links to a credential page, and are often disguised as invoices, receipts, resumes, or shipping notices to match a plausible pretext.

HTML smuggling is a technique in which an attached or downloaded HTML file reconstructs a malicious payload locally in the browser using script, evading network inspection that only sees the seemingly benign HTML wrapper. Archive files and disk-image formats are also used to nest the real payload and slip past simple attachment filters.

Dangerous patterns include attachments that prompt the user to enable content or macros, double extensions that disguise an executable as a document, password-protected archives whose password is in the email body to defeat scanning, and unexpected files from unfamiliar senders.

Defenses include disabling macros by default, opening untrusted documents in protected or sandboxed views, blocking high-risk file types at the gateway, and educating users that enabling content on an unsolicited document is a high-risk action.

title: Smishing (SMS) and Vishing (Voice) Phishing
text:
Phishing is not limited to email. Smishing uses SMS or messaging apps to deliver lures, exploiting the brevity of text messages - where full URLs and sender identity are hard to inspect - and the higher trust users place in their phones. Common themes include failed package deliveries, bank-fraud alerts, and toll or fee notices, each linking to a credential page or prompting a reply.

Vishing uses voice calls, often combined with caller-ID spoofing to display a trusted number. Attackers impersonate bank fraud departments, technical support, or government agencies and walk the victim through disclosing codes or installing remote-access software. Some campaigns combine channels, texting first and then calling to reinforce the pretext.

Generative voice cloning has made impersonation of specific individuals more convincing, raising the stakes for any request to move money or share codes received by phone.

The same principles apply across channels: be suspicious of unsolicited urgency, never share one-time codes with a caller, and verify any request independently by contacting the organization through its official published number rather than one provided in the message.

title: Email Authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
text:
Three complementary standards let receiving servers judge whether a message genuinely comes from the domain it claims. SPF (Sender Policy Framework) publishes, in DNS, the list of servers authorized to send mail for a domain, so a receiver can check whether the sending server is permitted. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) attaches a cryptographic signature to the message, allowing the receiver to verify that specified headers and the body were not altered and that they were signed by the domain's key.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) ties the two together by requiring alignment between the authenticated domain and the visible From domain, and it lets a domain owner publish a policy - none, quarantine, or reject - telling receivers what to do with messages that fail. DMARC also provides aggregate reporting so owners can see who is sending on their behalf.

Together these greatly reduce direct domain spoofing, which is why attackers increasingly pivot to lookalike domains they legitimately control - those domains can pass their own SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks while still deceiving the reader.

For defenders, a DMARC failure on a message impersonating a protected brand is a strong fraud indicator, but a DMARC pass only proves the message was authorized by its actual sending domain, not that the domain is trustworthy.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication, MFA Fatigue, and Phishing-Resistant Auth
text:
Multi-factor authentication adds a second proof of identity beyond a password and blocks the majority of commodity credential-stuffing and basic phishing. However, not all factors are equal. One-time codes by SMS or authenticator app can be phished in real time: a reverse-proxy kit relays the victim's code to the real site within its validity window.

MFA fatigue, or push-bombing, exploits app-based approval prompts by sending a flood of push notifications until a worn-down or confused user approves one. Number-matching and contextual prompts mitigate this but do not eliminate the social-engineering angle.

Phishing-resistant authentication based on the FIDO2 and WebAuthn standards - security keys and passkeys - binds the credential cryptographically to the legitimate site's origin, so it simply will not authenticate against a lookalike phishing domain. This origin binding is what makes it resistant rather than merely strong.

The practical guidance is to prefer phishing-resistant factors for high-value accounts, to be deeply suspicious of unexpected MFA prompts, and never to approve a prompt or read out a code that the user did not personally initiate.

title: Defensive Best Practices and Incident Response After a Phishing Attack
text:
Day-to-day defense rests on a few habits. Treat unsolicited messages that create urgency with suspicion. Inspect links before clicking by examining the registrable domain, and prefer navigating to services through bookmarks or typed addresses rather than embedded links. Never enter credentials or share one-time codes on a page or call reached through a message. Keep software and browsers updated, and enable phishing-resistant MFA where available.

Organizations layer additional controls: email authentication enforcement, link and attachment sandboxing, least-privilege access, and an easy, blame-free way for users to report suspicious messages, since fast reporting shortens the window of exposure for everyone.

If a user suspects they have been phished, speed matters. They should immediately change the password for the affected account and any account sharing that password, and revoke active sessions where the service allows it. Enabling or re-validating MFA, reviewing recent account activity and forwarding rules, and notifying the organization's security team or the impersonated institution are the next steps.

For financial fraud, contacting the bank or payment provider quickly can sometimes reverse or halt a transfer. Preserving the original message aids investigation and helps protect other potential targets.

title: How Machine-Learning Phishing Detection Works
text:
Automated phishing detection typically combines a text model and a URL model because the two carry different evidence. A transformer-based text model, such as a fine-tuned RoBERTa, reads email or message content and learns the linguistic patterns of social engineering - urgency, credential requests, impersonation - rather than matching fixed keywords, which lets it generalize to unseen wording.

A URL model operates on engineered features of the link and hostname: length and structure, character distribution, use of an IP address instead of a name, number of subdomains, presence of suspicious tokens, and reputation or age signals. Gradient-boosted decision trees such as XGBoost are well suited to this kind of structured tabular feature set and are fast at inference.

Calibrating a model's raw score into a meaningful probability, for instance with isotonic regression, makes the confidence value interpretable and lets a deployment choose an operating threshold that balances false positives against missed attacks.

Explainability methods such as SHAP attribute a prediction to the inputs that drove it - for a text model, the specific tokens that pushed the score toward phishing - which turns an opaque score into a human-readable rationale. Pairing detection with retrieval over a threat-intelligence knowledge base lets a system ground its explanation in established indicators, citing why a given pattern is considered risky rather than asserting it without support.
